                   JUDY GRACI'S REPLY TO APPLICANTS' EXCEPTIONS

                               TO THE PROPOSAL FOR DECISION

        Judy Graci, (Ms. Graci) appearing pro se, files this Reply to the Exceptions to the Proposal

for Decision ("PFD") filed by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission

Services Corporation (collectively, "Applicants") in PUC Docket No. 59475. In accordance with

the applicable procedural rules governing replies to exceptions, this Reply addresses Applicants'

exceptions in the order Applicants raised them, states the evidence and law relied upon with

particularity, and groups Ms. Graci' s arguments under the specific exceptions to which they

respond.



I. INTRODUCTION

        Applicants ask the Commission to treat ERCOT's Permian Basin Reliability Plan

( " PBRP") recommendation as functionally conclusive on need. But "great weight" is deference

owed to a recommendation lawfully produced - not a rule that immunizes a study from scrutiny.

PBRP built its need on a load case that excluded roughly 142,000 MW of load data PURA §

37.056(c-1) required ERCOT to consider. It also rested its largest non-oil and gas component on

unconfirmed officer-letter projections that ERCOT's own subsequent methodology correction

shows were substantially overstated. A study built on that record cannot be the "need" showing

PURA § 37.056 requires. The PFD's recommendation of denial should be affirmed, and the

Commission should deny the CCN applications in Docket No. 59475 and 59182.

 II. REPLY TO APPLICANTS' EXCEPTIONS

A. Reply to Applicants' Exception That the PFD Improperly Credits "Non-Expert" Lay

Opinion Over ERCOT's Technical Analysis.

         Applicants except to the PFD on the ground that it "affords greater weight to the opinion

testimony of lay witnesses... than it does to the consistent, well-documented recommendations of

ERCOT," and that the ALJs improperly "substitute their own load-forecasting and grid-planning

opinions for the regulatory framework."2

         The ALJs did not purport to second-guess ERCOT's power-flow modeling, contingency

analysis, or engineering judgment applied to the PBRP's chosen inputs. Their "changed

circumstances" finding rested on the record before them - principally the reduction in forecasted

non-oil-and-gas       load produced by applying                ERCOT's corrected 2025            load-forecasting

methodology, discussed in Section D below - that required no reweighing of ERCOT's

engineering judgment to reach.

          Applicants' related contention that the PFD's recommendation is an "outlier" because other

presiding officers reached different conclusions in Docket Nos. 59029, 59315, and 593363

         Likewise misstates the ALJs' role. An ALJ's obligation is to rule on the record actually

developed in the docket before that ALJ, not to reconcile the outcome with other dockets decided

on different records. To the extent this docket reached a different recommendation, the explanation

is that this record contains evidence - including the facility-by-facility load-validation evidence

and ERCOT's own admissions regarding its load-forecast methodology discussed below - that

GRACI 59475 & 59182 - Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                       Page 3 of 13
 was not before the presiding officers in those other dockets. A different, better-developed record

supporting a different recommendation is not an "outlier"; it is the adjudicative process working

as intended.



B. Reply to Applicants' Exception That the PBRP Alone Establishes Need Because It Was

Approved as an Integrated Plan.

         Applicants argue that the Commission and "six presiding officers across three other

dockets" have already found the PBRP sufficient to establish need, and that this finding "applies

with equal force to the Import Path 2 Projects, which are an integrated component of the same

reliability plan."4

         PURA § 37.051 requires a separate certificate of convenience and necessity for each

transmission facility, and PURA § 37.056 frames the necessity inquiry around whether "the

certificate" - not a regional plan in the abstract - is necessary for public service,

accommodation, convenience, or safety. That is why the PBRP produced five separate CCN

dockets rather than one omnibus filing. The "great weight" rule discussed in Section C below

affords ERCOT's package recommendation                      evidentiary     weight toward each individual

determination; it does not substitute for that determination. Applicants' position - that no

independent showing should ever be required for Import Path 2 because other Import Path dockets

reached a favorable result - would mean no individual PBRP line could ever be denied on need

grounds, since every line in a coordinated plan is, by definition, one piece of a larger package.

That cannot be the law the Legislature enacted when it required a separate certificate, under a

facility-specific necessity standard, for each line.


4Applicants' Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 7 ("First, the Commission and six presiding officers across
three other dockets have already found that the [PBRP] alone is sufficient to establish the need...").


GRACI 59475 & 59182 - Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                       Page 4 of 13
 C. Reply to Applicants' Exception That the PFD Erred in Declining to Give ERCOT's

Recommendation "Great Weight."

        Applicants except to the PFD's conclusion that ERCOT's PBRP recommendation is not

entitled to "great weight" under 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II), characterizing that

rule as non-discretionary. 5

        The rule is not disputed; its application here is. "Great weight" presumes a recommendation

lawfully produced; it is not automatic deference that survives proof that the underlying study

omitted the load data PURA § 37.056(c-1) required. Applicants note that ERCOT "continues to

recommend the Import Path 2 Projects notwithstanding" its later methodology change, as reflected

in the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP, and the April 2026 GTC exit strategy, and argue this shows the

methodology change "did not withdraw, amend, or supersede the PBRP." That observation does

not help Applicants: repeating the PBRP's conclusion in later planning documents does not cure

the input error that produced it, because none of those later documents' re-tests the PBRP's own

load assumptions against the complete, corrected statewide record. "Great weight" owed to a

recommendation is not increased by the number of times the recommendation is repeated without

re-examination.



D. Reply to Applicants' Exception Regarding "Changed Circumstances" and the PBRP's

Load Forecast (FOFs 87-111; COLs 13, 14).

        The PFD found that applying ERCOT's corrected load-forecasting methodology to the

PBRP's non-oil-and-gas projections "would result in a material reduction to the forecasted non-oil




~Applicants' Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 7-8; 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii)(II)


GRACI 59475 & 59182 - Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                      Page 5 of 13
 and gas load of at least 3,571 MW," and compared that figure to Import Path 2's safe loading limit

of5,270 MW.6

        Applicants assign five independent errors to this finding: that it overlooks the PBRP's

reliability methodology and planned-generation assumptions; that it treats the 2025 RTP

methodology as retroactive; that it discounts real historical load growth; that it gives dispositive

effect to lay opinion testimony; and that it disregards HB 5066's statutory framework. Each is

addressed below.7

        First, on the retroactivity point: Applicants state that "neither the Commission's order

approving that methodology nor the 2025 RTP indicate that the Commission intended its adoption

to retroactively revise the PBRP load forecasts downward."8

        That argument answers a procedural question the Commission was never asked to decide

and ignores the substantive one that controls here. Whether a corrected methodology is applied

retroactively to reopen a prior docket is a question of administrative process. Whether the data

underlying that prior docket was reliable in the first place is a question offact. ERCOT's own basis

for adjusting its methodology was a factual finding, publicly stated to its own Board, that TDSP

officer-letter data produces a load forecast so unrealistic that basing 2025 RTP base cases on the

raw officer-letter total - 218 GW - was not workable given "incomplete, inconsistent, and non-

standardized processes from the TDSPs."

ERCOT, Update on ERCOT's Adjusted Load Forecast and Request for Good Cause Exception,

PUCT Project No. 55999 (2025), at 1-2.

         Unreliable data does not become reliable merely because the finding of unreliability was

announced after, rather than before, a particular study relied on it. The magnitude of the correction

confirms the point: ERCOT's adjusted methodology reduces all TSP officer-letter loads to 55.4

percent of the TSP-sponsored amount and further reduces data-center loads within that category

to 49.8 percent of the already-reduced amount - meaning data-center loads reported in TSP

officer letters count for only approximately 27.6 percent ofwhat TSPs originally represented.

        Reports of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Project No. 55999, Order Granting

Good Cause Exception at 1 (Jun. 5, 2025).9

        Applicants observe that this specific percentage reduction "applies only to ERCOT's

calculation of data center loads that are not supported by an interconnection agreement and are

reflected only in a TSP officer-letter for the purpose of establishing the base load in ERCOT's 2025

RTP" and does not, by its terms, govern the PBRP. That is true as a matter of the order's formal

scope. But it is not a reason to ignore the finding for purposes of evaluating the PBRP's reliability

as evidence. The corrected methodology exists because ERCOT concluded, based on "historical

realized information," that officer-letter and data-center load figures of the same type and

provenance as those underlying the PBRP's own non-oil-and-gas forecast substantially overstate

real demand. Nor is there any principled reason a capital commitment of this magnitude - the

three 765-kV import paths comprising the PBRP, across five CCN dockets, carry a combined

estimated cost of approximately $11 billion - should escape re-evaluation under a corrected

methodology simply because the flawed study happened to be completed first. If the same defect

that justified adjusting officer-letter and data-center loads for the 2025 RTP infects the PBRP's

own load forecast, the age of the study is a reason for more scrutiny before committing ratepayers


9Applicants' Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 14 (citing Order Granting Good Cause Exception at 1 (Jun.
5,2025)).


GRACI 59475 & 59182 - Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                     Page 7 of 13
 to billions of dollars in cost recovery, not a basis for exempting it from the scrutiny ERCOT itself

has already applied elsewhere.

         Second, on planned-generation assumptions: Applicants note that ERCOT modeled

approximately 17 GW of planned generation in the PBRP, and that even after adding a further 11

GW of unplanned generation to balance the contemporaneous 2024 RTP, ERCOT still identified

the 765-kV import paths as necessary. 10

         This proves less than Applicants suggest. That the 2024 RTP required an additional 11 GW

of unplanned generation to balance - on top of the PBRP's own 17,170 MW -is further evidence

that the PBRP's Permian-only load case was itself out of step with the statewide load and

generation picture ERCOT was contemporaneously developing. It does not rehabilitate the PBRP's

load forecast; it is additional confirmation of the same gap identified throughout this Reply.

         Third, on the argument that the PFD improperly credits lay opinion over technical analysis:

the finding the ALJs actually relied on - that ERCOT's own corrected methodology would reduce

the PBRP's non-oil-and-gas forecast by at least 3,571 MW against a 5,270 MW safe loading limit

- rests on ERCOT's own Commission-approved order, not on lay speculation about power-flow

modeling. Crediting ERCOT's own admissions is not crediting unqualified opinion. The additional

generation-balance comparison Intervenor requests the Commission judicially notice, see Section

A, supra, likewise rests entirely on ERCOT's own official planning documents and requires no

technical opinion testimony to understand it is a comparison oftwo totals ERCOT itself published

in the same year.




loApplicants' Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 13-14 (citing Applicants' Ex. 17 (Gurley Reb.), Ex. JG-R--2
at 18-19 (2024 RTP)).


GRACI 59475 & 59182 - Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                                       Page 8 of 13
 Fourth, on HB 5066's statutory framework and PURA §§ 39.166(b) and 37.057's directive that the

PBRP be completed expeditiously: 11

        Expedition is not a substitute for accuracy. PURA § 37.056(c-1) requires the Commission

to consider historical load, forecasted load growth, and additional load currently seeking

interconnection - it does not instruct the Commission to accept incomplete or overstated forecasts

in the interest of speed. A statutory directive to move quickly does not repeal the statutory

requirement to get the underlying numbers right.

        The PFD's changed-circumstances finding is not limited to the non-oil-and-gas forecast.

The PFD also found that the PBRP's oil-and-gas load forecast is undermined by intervening

changes to federal methane regulation that have reduced the regulatory pressure originally driving

oilfield electrification in the Permian Basin. 12

        A principal driver of the electrification assumed in the PBRP's oil-and-gas forecast was

operators' need to reduce flaring and venting to comply with the U. S. Environmental Protection

Agency's 2024 methane rules; electrifying compressors and other field equipment was one-way

operators reduced routine flaring rather than face associated compliance costs. That regulatory

pressure has since eased. On April 6, 2026, EPA finalized a rule revising its 2024 methane

regulations to provide operators "flexibility" by loosening flaring and vent-gas requirements, and

on May 1, 2026, EPA issued guidance clarifying that operators may continue flaring in

circumstances the 2024 rule's original deadline would have foreclosed. 13

        Separately, in March 2025 Congress invoked the Congressional Review Act to prohibit

EPA from collecting the methane Waste Emissions Charge established under the Inflation

 Reduction Act until 2034, removing a further cost incentive for electrification that was in place

when the PBRP's oil-and-gas load forecast was developed. 14

         Because a substantial share ofthe PBRP's forecasted oil-and-gas load growth was premised

on continued, and increasing, methane-driven electrification, the subsequent relaxation ofthe very

regulations that were driving that electrification independently undermines the reliability of the

PBRP's oil-and-gas forecast - reinforcing, on this additional and separate basis already reflected

in the PFD, the ALJs' conclusion that changed circumstances have undermined the need Applicants

ask the Commission to find.

         Fifth, and independent of the five errors Applicants themselves identify, the actual

historical peak-demand figures Applicants' own witness supplies do not match ERCOT's own

settled load data for the Far West weather zone, which is the zone most directly comparable to the

Permian Basin service territory at issue. Applicants' testimony reports a 2023 Far West peak of

approximately 6,900 MW and a 2025 Far West peak of approximately 9,800 MW.15

         ERCOT's own settled hourly load data for the Far West zone - the actual, metered record

ERCOT itself publishes - shows a 2023 peak of 6,640 MW, occurring August 13, 2023, and a

peak of 8,725 MW, occurring July 24, 2026.16

         Applicants' reported figures accordingly overstate ERCOT's own actual 2023 peak by

approximately 260 MW, or 3.9 percent, and overstate ERCOT's own actual 2025 peak by

approximately 1,027 MW, or 11.7 percent. A witness whose historical peak-demand figures run

measurably above ERCOT's own contemporaneously metered record for the same zone provides

an independent reason to question the reliability of those witness' forward-looking projections,

 which is precisely the reliability question at the center of this Reply. The Commission need not

resolve why the discrepancy exists - whether through a different zone definition, a different

measurement methodology, or otherwise - to recognize that a forecast is only as trustworthy as

the historical baseline it is built from, and here the historical baseline itself does not match the

public record.



E. Reply to Applicants' Exception That the Far West Texas Import GTCs Independently

Establish Need Regardless of Load Forecast.

        Applicants argue that the Far West Texas Import Generic Transmission Constraints

("GTCs") demonstrate need "today, regardless ofwhether additional load materializes," citing an

imminent threat of firm load shed exceeding 2,000 MW and ERCOT's April 2026 exit strategy

identifying all three import paths as essential to retiring the GTCs by 2030 even assuming

approximately 2,500 MW of new dispatchable generation. 17

         The GTCs reflect a real, present strain on the existing 345-kV system. But that constraint

does not establish that these specific 765-kV facilities - sized to a load level the PBRP cannot

reliably support, for the reasons set out in Section D above - are necessary by 2030, as opposed

to a smaller, faster, or differently sequenced reinforcement matched to verified demand. Correcting

the load side ofERCOT's own exit-strategy analysis for the forecast defects identified in this Reply

may support a smaller or later solution than the one Applicants propose. Substantial local

reinforcement is, in any event, already proceeding independent of Import Path 2: the PBRP's

separate "local upgrade" portfolio - more than 500 miles of 345-kV and 138-kV lines across the

Permian and Delaware Basins, several already independently CCN-approved - is scheduled for



17Applicants' Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 8-9.


GRACI 59475 & 59182 - Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                        Page 11 of 13
 completion on substantially the same 2026-2030 timeline, regardless of the outcome here.

Denying this application does not leave the region without near-term relief.




F. Reply to Applicants' Exception Regarding Generation Alternatives and the Adequacy of

Alternatives Analysis.

         Applicants except to the PFD's reliance on evidence that approximately 39 GW of

generation has been announced in the Permian Basin, arguing that only 1.35 GW was under

construction as of May 2026, that some identified generators would not even interconnect with

ERCOT, and that ERCOT's planning already accounted for planned generation. 18

         The identical critique applies with equal force to the load forecast Applicants ask the

Commission to credit. If uncertainty about whether announced generation will be built in time is

a reason to discount that evidence, uncertainty about whether officer-letter and data-center load

will materialize as forecast - the same category of data ERCOT's own corrected methodology

found to be substantially overstated - is a reason to discount the PBRP's demand forecast on the

opposite side of the same ledger. Applicants cannot ask the Commission to discount speculative

generation on evidentiary grounds while simultaneously asking it to accept an equally speculative,

and independently shown to be overstated, load forecast at face value.

        Nor does comparing 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV configurations constitute an alternatives

analysis. Every option in that comparison is still new transmission; it answers what size line to

build, not whether new transmission is necessary compared to non-transmission alternatives such

as new in-basin generation or demand-side measures. Any such comparison is only as reliable as

the demand it is sized to meet, and an inflated target will always make the largest available solution



18Applicants' Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision at 9.


GRACI 59475 & 59182 - Reply Exceptions to Proposal for Decision                          Page 12 of 13
 look necessary. The market's own conduct confirms credible non-transmission alternatives exist:

Chevron, the second-largest Permian producer, is building a 2.5 GW gas plant, expandable to 5

GW, under a twenty-year power supply agreement with Microsoft, targeted online in 2027 - a

named supermajor, a named hyperscale counterparty, and a signed twenty-year term.



III. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

        For the foregoing reasons, Ms. Graci respectfully requests that the Commission overrule

Applicants' Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision and adopt the ALJs' recommendation that the

CCN application in Docket No. 59475 and 59182 be denied for failure to establish need under

PURA § 37.056. Ms. Grad further requests any additional relief to which it may be justly entitled.




Respectfully submitted,
